issues.legal_issue: A writing that records a previously completed partition and lists the properties allotted to each side is not an instrument of partition requiring registration.
material_facts: The agricultural properties had already been divided between the two family branches, and their respective shares had been entered separately in the revenue records, disrupting their joint status.
The writing described the residential properties and other remaining properties allotted to each branch and began by recording that the parties had discussed and mutually agreed on the arrangement.
The parties disputed their respective claims to the properties, and the writing recorded the arrangement rather than itself effecting a change in their legal relations.
issues.conclusion: The writing was a memorandum recording a past arrangement, not an instrument that itself effected partition; it did not require registration and was admissible in evidence to prove the partition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, a document requires registration when it itself operates or purports to operate to create or declare rights in immovable property. A writing that merely records a completed partition, or is only a list of properties allotted, does not require registration. A document that itself effects division and embodies the terms of the bargain must be registered, and if it is not, Section 49 excludes it from evidence; secondary evidence of that partition is also barred by Section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The Court relied on Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar, Nani Bai v. Gita Bai, and the principles discussed in Narayan Sakharam Patil v. Cooperative Central Bank, Bageshwari Charan Singh v. Jagarnath Kuari, and Subramanian v. Lutchman.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a writing that records a past arrangement and lists allocated properties after the parties have already separated their joint status, the writing may be admitted without registration to prove the partition.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered record of a partition may be used for a limited collateral purpose to show severance in status and the character of possession.
material_facts: The writing recorded the parties’ arrangement concerning the division of the remaining family properties after agricultural lands had been partitioned and the family’s joint status disrupted.
The parties subsequently divided and possessed properties in accordance with the intention to divide recorded in the writing.
The writing was relied on to show the nature and character of possession of the properties allotted to the family members.
issues.conclusion: Even if unregistered, the writing could be considered for the limited collateral purpose of establishing severance in status and showing that the subsequent division of the properties followed the original intention to divide.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 permits an otherwise inadmissible unregistered document to be used as evidence of a collateral transaction not required to be effected by a registered instrument. Such a document may be used for the limited purpose of showing severance in status and the resulting nature of possession, but not to prove a transfer of legal title. The Court relied on Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal and referred to the principles in Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar and Nani Bai v. Gita Bai.

issues.legal_issue: A family settlement resolving competing claims based on antecedent title does not require registration when it does not transfer or declare an interest for the first time.
material_facts: The family members asserted competing claims to the properties and adjusted those claims by agreement.
The settlement proceeded on the basis that the parties had antecedent titles to the properties and acknowledged and defined the titles of those receiving particular properties.
The arrangement settled the competing claims rather than transferring title from a person with absolute title to other parties.
issues.conclusion: The family arrangement did not create or declare an interest in property for the first time and did not require registration.
issues.legal_principle: Where a person with absolute title transfers title in property to others, the legal formalities for that transfer must be complied with. By contrast, where parties assert competing titles and a compromise resolves their claims on the footing of antecedent title, no party derives title from another and the arrangement does not create or declare an interest for the first time. The Court relied on Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Khunni Lal v. Gobind Krishna Narain, and Lalla Oudh Behari Lall v. Mewa Koonwar.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal.

issues.definition: When a family settlement adjusts competing claims based on antecedent titles without a transfer between the parties, the settlement does not require registration.
